blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation. Evaluation both guides subsequent search and determines the final scaffold, but evaluating every candidate on the full task set incurs substantial execution costs. We investigate how evaluation budgets can be allocated across these two roles. Our experiments show that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while additional targeted evaluation improves final selection. Replay analyses further show that shared informative items and a common scoring reference support comparisons among closely matched candidates. Motivated by these findings, we propose \method, an evaluation allocation framework that combines sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation. A short fully evaluated warm-up establishes a shared informative core and calibrates a response model whose item parameters remain fixed during search. After search, \method refits the model and applies paired successive halving, reusing accumulated observations and executing only missing evaluations. Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, \method achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells.

blocks.en: 1. Introduction
blocks.zh: 一、导 言 导言

blocks.en:
A scaffold for a large language model (LLM) agent is an
executable program that defines how an agent coordinates
LLM calls, maintains intermediate state, and interacts
with tools and external information
sources ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) .
For Web-facing agents, scaffolds govern how agents acquire
and use information through Web searches, document
retrieval, and interactions with online
services ( Nakano et al., 2021 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) .
While these scaffolds have traditionally been designed
and refined manually, recent advances have enabled
their automated optimization ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) .
For example, ShinkaEvolve ( Lange et al., 2026 ) iteratively
proposes scaffold modifications and uses evaluation
feedback to guide subsequent evolution.

blocks.en:
However, evaluating candidate scaffolds can incur
substantial execution costs. A single task instance
may involve multiple LLM calls, retrieval steps,
and tool interactions ( Mialon et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) ,
making full evaluation across many candidates expensive.
Although parallel evaluation and asynchronous program
generation can overlap computation ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ) ,
feedback-dependent search decisions still require
evaluation results.
Existing approaches reduce evaluation costs through
sparse score estimation and evaluation
cascades ( Fisch et al., 2026 ; Gideoni et al., 2026 ) , treating evaluation
primarily as a fitness-estimation problem.
In scaffold evolution, however, evaluation supports
two distinct decisions: it provides fitness feedback
that shapes archive updates and subsequent
proposals ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , and it determines
which scaffold is ultimately returned.
These decisions impose different requirements:
search benefits from inexpensive yet comparable
feedback, whereas final selection requires reliable
discrimination among competitive candidates.
This raises a central question: How should a limited evaluation budget be
allocated across these two decisions to improve
the quality of the ultimately selected scaffold?

blocks.en:
To answer this question, we investigate how evaluation
allocation affects evolutionary search and final
scaffold selection. Our investigation yields three
findings.
First, sparse evaluation feedback can sustain
productive evolution, whereas removing feedback
substantially degrades search quality.
Second, shared informative items improve comparisons
between closely matched candidates, while maintaining
a common scoring reference helps preserve comparability
across evolutionary iterations.
Third, search improvements are concentrated in early
iterations, whereas final selection remains sensitive
to uncertainty among top candidates.
These findings suggest that evaluation
should provide inexpensive yet comparable feedback
during search, while reserving additional observations
for final selection.

blocks.en:
Motivated by these findings, we propose EvalAlloc ,
an evaluation allocation framework that separates
sparse search-time feedback from targeted final
selection. During search, a short fully evaluated
warm-up identifies a shared informative core and
calibrates a response model. Subsequent candidates
are evaluated on sparse item sets centered on this
core, while the model’s item parameters remain fixed
to maintain a common scoring reference for archive
updates and parent selection.
After search, EvalAlloc applies warm-started paired
successive halving (SH), reusing accumulated
observations and performing only missing evaluations.
A refitted response model further supports
comparisons during later selection rounds.
We evaluate EvalAlloc on four benchmarks and two
evolution frameworks, with three independent runs
per setting. Compared with full evaluation, EvalAlloc uses approximately half as many evaluation cells
while achieving competitive or higher mean
performance across the evaluated settings.
Ablation studies further show that informative
item allocation and final selection are the
main contributors to its effectiveness.
These results demonstrate the benefits of separating
sparse search-time feedback from targeted final
evaluation.

model, and warm-started paired successive
halving to allocate evaluation effort across
evolutionary search and final selection. • We evaluate EvalAlloc across four
benchmarks and two evolution frameworks,
complemented by controlled replay analyses,
demonstrating competitive final performance
with substantially fewer evaluation cells.

blocks.en: 2. Related Work
blocks.zh: 2. 相关工作

blocks.en:
LLM-Driven Agent and Program Evolution. Recent work has explored the automated design and
optimization of agent scaffolds and executable
workflows using LLMs ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) .
ADAS ( Hu et al., 2025 ) uses a meta-agent to generate
agent programs based on previous discoveries, while
AFlow ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) employs Monte Carlo Tree
Search to optimize code-represented workflows.
Other approaches, including
ShinkaEvolve ( Lange et al., 2026 ) and
AdaEvolve ( Cemri et al., 2026 ) , iteratively generate,
evaluate, and refine programs using evaluation
feedback to guide subsequent search.
These approaches primarily focus on improving
candidate generation and evolutionary optimization.
Our work instead examines the evaluation process
underlying this feedback-driven search, studying how
limited evaluation resources can support both
evolutionary decisions and final scaffold selection.

blocks.en:
Efficient LLM Evaluation. Reducing the cost of evaluating LLMs has received
growing attention.
Methods such as tinyBenchmarks ( Polo et al., 2024 ) use carefully selected examples and statistical
estimation to approximate full-benchmark performance,
while SparseEval ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) optimizes
representative items for efficient score estimation
and ranking.
CollabEval ( Fisch et al., 2026 ) exploits shared information
across evaluations through matrix completion to
improve statistical efficiency.
Growing Pains ( Habba et al., 2026 ) uses fixed
item-response calibration and anchor items to
maintain score comparability across evaluation
periods.
These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of
sparse observations and response modeling.
However, in scaffold evolution, evaluation estimates
also influence archive updates and subsequent
candidate generation.
Therefore, we examine not only estimation
accuracy, but also how shared informative observations
and stable scoring references support reliable
evolutionary decisions.

blocks.en:
Evaluation Allocation and Candidate Selection. Evaluation allocation is closely related to
sequential resource allocation and best-arm
identification.
Successive halving ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) and Hyperband ( Li et al., 2018 ) progressively
concentrate evaluation resources on promising
candidates, while racing-based methods such as
irace ( López-Ibáñez et al., 2016 ) eliminate weaker
configurations through sequential comparisons.
Common random numbers ( Glasserman and Yao, 1992 ) provide a classical motivation for evaluating
alternatives under shared conditions to reduce
the variance of pairwise comparisons.
Recent analyses of code evolution ( Gideoni et al., 2026 ) also highlight the importance of reliable candidate
evaluation and selection.
Building on these ideas, our work studies evaluation
allocation across two distinct stages:
providing inexpensive yet comparable feedback
during evolution and reusing accumulated observations
for reliable final scaffold selection.

blocks.en: 4.1. Setup

We study four benchmarks: HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , HoVer ( Jiang et al., 2020 ) ,
DROP ( Dua et al., 2019 ) , and IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2026 ) .
Each benchmark is divided into SEARCH (300 items), DEV (150 items),
and TEST (300 items, except 294 for IFBench), as shown in Table 1 .
SEARCH is used for evolution and final selection, DEV for auxiliary audits, and TEST exclusively for evaluating
the selected scaffolds.
We use two evolution frameworks: ShinkaEvolve ( Lange et al., 2026 ) and AdaEvolve ( Cemri et al., 2026 ) , the latter implemented using
SkyDiscover ( Liu et al., 2026 ) .
Each run makes 80 proposals from the same initial program, with three seeds per setting.
We use Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) as the executor, with temperature zero, thinking disabled, and at most 16,384 output tokens, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 ( Xu et al., 2026 ) as the proposer.
Both models are served locally with vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) on a single node with eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs.

blocks.en: Figure 3. Overview of EvalAlloc . The framework consists of three stages: (1) core calibration using fully evaluated warm-up candidates, (2) sparse search-time evaluation with a shared informative core and fixed response model, and (3) warm-started successive halving that reuses accumulated observations for final scaffold selection.

blocks.en:
Figure 3 illustrates EvalAlloc , an evaluation allocation framework that distributes evaluation effort across three stages: Core Calibration , Shared-Core Evolution , and Warm-Started Selection . EvalAlloc decouples the two roles of evaluation: search-time feedback only needs to be cheap and comparable enough to guide evolution, whereas the final choice needs precise comparisons among the strongest candidates.
It therefore splits one evaluation budget into a sparse search stage and a separate selection stage that reuses every observation collected during search.
The key idea is to invest a small evaluation budget upfront to establish a reusable reference, use shared informative items to provide comparable feedback throughout evolution, and concentrate additional evaluations on final scaffold selection. EvalAlloc operates as a drop-in evaluator, leaving the native framework’s proposal, archive, and parent-selection policies unchanged.

blocks.en: 6. Experiments
blocks.zh: 6. 实验

blocks.en: 6.1. Setup

Baselines. We compare EvalAlloc against five evaluation strategies with different budget allocations. Skip Eval performs no evaluation during either search or final selection, and select the last valid evolved program. Successive Halving (SH) ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) provides no evaluation feedback during search and applies successive halving to the generated candidate pool for final selection. Random evaluates each candidate on a randomly sampled 50% subset of SEARCH items. Cascade ( Novikov et al., 2025 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) first evaluates candidates on 20% of SEARCH items and promotes candidates meeting a top-25% threshold to full evaluation, while allocating no additional evaluations to the remaining candidates. Full evaluates every candidate on all SEARCH items.

Cascade(Novikov等人,2025年;Agrawal等人,2026年)首先对20%的SEARCH项目对候选人进行评审,推动达到最高-25%临界值的候选人接受全面评审,同时不向其余候选人追加评审. 全面评价SEARCH所有项目的所有候选人。

Unless otherwise specified, EvalAlloc allocates 30% of the full-evaluation budget to search, with the first W = 10 W=10 valid candidates fully evaluated and each subsequent candidate evaluated on k = 60 k=60 items (20% of SEARCH).

blocks.en: 6.2. Main Results
blocks.zh: 6.2. 主要成果

blocks.en:
Table 3 compares the TEST performance and evaluation cost of different strategies.
Across both evolution frameworks and all four benchmarks, EvalAlloc matches or slightly exceeds the mean TEST score of Full while using approximately half as many evaluation cells.
It also outperforms Random and Cascade in cross-benchmark average performance at comparable or lower evaluation cost.
These results demonstrate that allocating evaluations selectively can provide a better cost–performance tradeoff than uniformly evaluating candidates.
The evaluation costs differ between the two frameworks partly due to their handling of invalid proposals.
AdaEvolve retries program generation when a proposal is invalid, whereas ShinkaEvolve discards invalid proposals without replacement.
Since invalid programs incur no evaluation cost, ShinkaEvolve evaluates fewer valid candidates, resulting in lower realized evaluation costs, particularly under Full evaluation.
blocks.zh:
表3比较了不同战略的TEST性能和评价成本。
从演化框架和所有四个基准来看,EvalAlloc匹配或略高于 " Full " 的TEST平均得分,同时使用大约一半的评价单元格。
它还以可比或较低的评价成本在跨基准平均业绩上超过了随机和连带。
这些结果显示,有选择地分配评价比统一评价候选人可以提供更好的成本-业绩权衡。
这两个框架的评价费用不同,部分原因是它们处理了无效的提议。
AdaEvolve在提案无效时重试程序生成,而ShinkaEvolve则在不替换的情况下丢弃无效的提案.
由于无效的程序不需要评估费用, Shinka 对有效候选人的评价减少,导致实际评价费用降低,特别是在全面评价下。

blocks.en:
The no-evaluation baselines further highlight the complementary roles of search feedback and final selection.
Applying SH to candidates generated without evaluation feedback substantially improves final performance, but still falls short of EvalAlloc .
This suggests that final selection can recover promising candidates even from unguided search, while informative feedback during evolution provides additional benefits.
These findings support combining sparse search-time evaluation with targeted final confirmation.
blocks.zh:
无评价基线进一步突出了搜索反馈和最后选择的互补作用。
将SH应用于没有评价反馈的候选人,大大改善了最终业绩,但仍低于EvalAlloc。
这表明,最终甄选即使从无指导的搜索中也能恢复有希望的候选人,而信息化期间的反馈则提供了额外好处。
这些调查结果支持将有限的搜索时间评价与目标明确的最后确认结合起来。

blocks.en: 6.3. Ablation Study
blocks.zh: 6.3. 读取研究

blocks.en:
We ablate three components of EvalAlloc on ShinkaEvolve across all four benchmarks. W/o selection skips final confirmation and selects the candidate with the highest refitted response-model estimate from the same search runs. W/o response model uses raw observed means for search feedback and raw union means for final selection. W/o informative items replaces informative item selection with random sampling while preserving the shared core and evaluation budget.
The latter two variants require new evolution runs because they change the search-time feedback.
blocks.zh:
我们放弃EvalAlloc在ShinkaEvolve上的三个组成部分,涵盖所有四项基准。 W/o选择跳过最终确认,并从同一搜索运行中选择重排响应模式估计最高的候选人. W/o响应模型使用原始观测手段进行搜索反馈,原始结合手段进行最终选择. W/o信息项目用随机抽样取代信息项目选择,同时保留共享的核心和评价预算。
后两种变体需要新的演化运行,因为它们改变了搜索时间反馈.

blocks.en:
Table 4 shows that removing final confirmation consistently reduces TEST performance, highlighting the importance of additional evaluation for selecting among competitive candidates.
Replacing informative items with random ones produces the largest average degradation, suggesting that sharing evaluation items alone is insufficient without considering their informativeness.
Removing the response model has a smaller and less consistent effect, as the shared core already provides substantial comparability among candidates.
The response model therefore primarily serves to calibrate sparse feedback onto a common scoring scale.
Overall, these results identify informative item selection and final confirmation as the main contributors to EvalAlloc .

表4显示,取消最后确认的做法始终会降低技术、技术和革新方面的业绩,突出显示在竞争性候选人中进行额外评价的重要性。
将资料性项目替换为随机性项目,造成最大的平均退化,说明单独分享评价项目是不够的,而不考虑其信息性。
取消反应模式的效果较小,也不太一致,因为共享的核心已经为候选人提供了实质性的可比性。
因此,反应模式主要有助于将有限的反馈校准到一个共同的评分尺度。
总的来说,这些结果确定了信息丰富的项目选择和最后确认是EvalAlloc的主要贡献者。

blocks.en: 6.4. Analysis

Budget Allocation in Warm-up Stage. Figure 4 examines the effect of warm-up length W W on DROP with ShinkaEvolve under a fixed search-stage budget.
A longer warm-up provides more observations for calibration but leaves fewer evaluation items for subsequent candidates.
The default W = 10 W=10 achieves the highest mean performance, although the differences are within seed-to-seed variation.
All three configurations outperform Random at comparable evaluation cost.
Offline replays further show that an excessively long warm-up reduces search-time ranking accuracy as later evaluations become too sparse.
These results highlight the trade-off between upfront calibration and informative feedback during subsequent evolution.

Budget Allocation in Search Stage. Figure 5 examines the effect of search-time evaluation budget on DROP with ShinkaEvolve.
We fix the warm-up at ten fully evaluated candidates and vary the target search budget from 20% to 40%.
The default 30% allocation achieves the highest observed mean TEST performance, while the 20% configuration offers comparable performance at lower cost.
Increasing the search-time budget does not consistently improve final performance in this setting, suggesting that sparse feedback can be sufficient to guide productive evolution.

Budget Allocation in Selection Stage. Figure 6 examines the effect of final confirmation budget while reusing the same search runs.
Compared with direct selection based on search-stage estimates, successive halving (SH) improves TEST performance across all four benchmarks.
Applying SH to the top 30 candidates captures most of the improvement at lower cost, while considering all candidates provides a modest additional gain.
These results highlight the value of targeted final confirmation and the trade-off between selection cost and final scaffold quality.

Higher-scoring candidates tend to consume more tokens

blocks.en: 7. Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7. 结论

blocks.en:
Evaluation influences both evolutionary search and
final scaffold selection.
Our investigation shows that sparse informative
feedback can guide evolution, while shared evaluation
items and a stable scoring reference support
comparable decisions across candidates.
Motivated by these findings, we propose EvalAlloc ,
which combines sparse search-time feedback with
warm-started final confirmation.
Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, EvalAlloc achieves competitive performance
while using approximately half as many evaluation
cells as Full.
These results highlight the importance of allocating
evaluation effort according to its distinct roles
in search and final selection.
